params.question: A 45-year-old man with foul-smelling ear discharge for ten years presents with sudden cessation of the discharge, followed by severe headache and confusion. What does the sudden drying of the ear most likely indicate?

answers.text: Spontaneous healing of the tympanic membrane perforation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Spontaneous healing of a long-standing perforation is uncommon. The new-onset headache and confusion indicate clinical deterioration, not recovery.

answers.text: Extension of infection toward the intracranial cavity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: In chronic suppurative otitis media, sudden cessation of discharge can mean the infection has sealed inward. Combined with headache and altered sensorium, this suggests intracranial spread — a life-threatening complication requiring urgent intervention.

answers.text: Resolution of the infection due to improved immunity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Spontaneous resolution of a decade-long infection without treatment is implausible. The accompanying headache and confusion are new symptoms indicating worsening, not resolution.

answers.text: Blockage of the ear canal by inspissated wax

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Wax impaction causes fullness or hearing loss but would not account for severe headache and altered consciousness. These point to a deeper complication.

overallFeedback.feedback: When chronic ear discharge suddenly stops and headache or confusion appears, the infection may have tracked inward toward the brain. This is a neurosurgical emergency, not clinical improvement.
In chronic suppurative otitis media, sudden cessation of discharge with new headache and confusion suggests intracranial extension of infection — this is an emergency, not a sign of improvement.

params.question: A 55-year-old smoker presents with severe left-sided ear pain. Otoscopy reveals a completely normal tympanic membrane. What is the most appropriate next step?

answers.text: Prescribe analgesics and review after two weeks

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Severe otalgia with a normal tympanic membrane is referred pain until proved otherwise. Delaying examination risks missing a tonsillar or tongue-base carcinoma, especially in a smoker.

answers.text: Order a CT scan of the temporal bone

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: CT of the temporal bone evaluates middle ear pathology. The normal tympanic membrane makes a middle-ear cause unlikely. Clinical examination of the pharynx and larynx should precede imaging.

answers.text: Examine the oropharynx, tongue base, and larynx

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Cranial nerves V, IX, and X and cervical roots C2–C3 supply the ear. Severe otalgia with a normal eardrum strongly suggests referred pain. In a smoker, oropharyngeal and laryngeal malignancy must be excluded by direct examination.
Antibiotic ear drops treat external or middle ear infection. With a normal tympanic membrane and canal, the pain source lies outside the ear — topical treatment will not address it.

overallFeedback.feedback: The ear is supplied by multiple cranial nerves (V, IX, X) and cervical roots (C2, C3). Severe ear pain with a normal eardrum means the source is elsewhere — examine the teeth, tonsils, tongue base, and larynx, especially in a smoker.
Severe otalgia with a normal tympanic membrane is referred pain. In a smoker, the oropharynx and larynx must be examined to exclude malignancy — a tonsillar carcinoma can present as ear pain alone.

interactions.label: A positive Rinne test always indicates normal hearing.

params.question: A positive Rinne test always indicates normal hearing.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: A positive Rinne test means air conduction exceeds bone conduction. This is seen in normal hearing AND in sensorineural hearing loss. Only conductive hearing loss produces a negative Rinne result. To distinguish normal from sensorineural loss, you need the Weber test and the absolute bone conduction test.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. Rinne positive means air conduction exceeds bone conduction. This occurs in both normal hearing and sensorineural hearing loss. The Rinne test only turns negative when there is conductive hearing loss — that is, when the middle ear mechanism itself is damaged.

interactions.label: A tympanogram shows a flat trace with no identifiable peak, and the measured ear

params.question: A tympanogram shows a flat trace with no identifiable peak, and the measured ear canal volume is significantly larger than normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A flat (Type B) tympanogram with a large ear canal volume indicates the probe is measuring the combined volume of the ear canal and the middle ear cleft through a perforation. No intact membrane is vibrating, hence no compliance peak.

Middle ear effusion also produces a flat (Type B) tympanogram, but with a normal ear canal volume. The significantly increased volume here indicates sound energy is escaping into the middle ear space through a perforation.
Otosclerosis produces a Type As tympanogram — a peak near zero decaPascals with reduced compliance (below 0.3 mL), reflecting ossicular chain stiffening. It does not produce a flat trace.
Eustachian tube dysfunction produces a Type C tympanogram — a clear peak shifted to negative pressure — not a flat trace. The negative pressure reflects impaired middle ear ventilation.

overallFeedback.feedback: Type B (flat) tympanograms have two key interpretations based on ear canal volume: normal volume suggests middle ear effusion; large volume indicates tympanic membrane perforation, as the probe measures the canal plus the middle ear space.
A flat tympanogram with a large ear canal volume means sound energy is escaping through a perforated tympanic membrane into the middle ear cleft, producing no compliance peak.

interactions.label: During oral examination of a chronic gutka chewer, you find a painless red velve

params.question: During oral examination of a chronic gutka chewer, you find a painless red velvety patch on the buccal mucosa that cannot be rubbed off. What should be your immediate course of action?

answers.text: Reassure the patient as the absence of pain suggests a benign condition

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The absence of pain is misleading. Early oral squamous cell carcinoma and high-risk premalignant lesions are characteristically painless. Pain indicates advanced infiltration, not the onset of malignancy.

answers.text: Prescribe topical antifungal agents and review in two weeks

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Antifungals treat oral candidiasis, which presents as white plaques that can be rubbed off, revealing a raw base. A red patch that cannot be rubbed off is erythroplakia, not candidiasis.

answers.text: Advise tobacco cessation and schedule review in six months

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Tobacco cessation is important but insufficient. Erythroplakia carries approximately 50% malignancy risk at biopsy — a six-month delay risks progression to invasive carcinoma.

Erythroplakia — a red velvety patch that cannot be rubbed off — carries approximately 50% malignancy risk at biopsy. The absence of pain does not exclude malignancy; early oral squamous cell carcinoma is classically painless. Urgent biopsy is mandatory.

overallFeedback.feedback: A red velvety patch (erythroplakia) that cannot be rubbed off is the highest-risk premalignant oral lesion, with approximately 50% malignancy at biopsy. Painlessness is characteristic of early oral malignancy, not a sign of benignity.
Erythroplakia demands urgent biopsy — it carries approximately 50% malignancy risk. Never be reassured by the absence of pain; early oral malignancy is characteristically painless.
